sections.h2: Hardin County Recorder location and hours
sections.html:
The Hardin County Recorder is at One Courthouse Square, Suite 220, Kenton, Ohio 43326. Dial 419-674-2252 or 419-674-2250, or fax 419-675-2802. The counter opens at half past eight and closes at four on weekdays.

The Auditor is in the same courthouse, Suite 250, at 419-674-2239, and keeps hours of 8:00 to 4:00 on weekdays. Since a conveyance has to touch both offices, a short walk down the hall is often how a deed gets done.

The Recorder's page links to an online search run through Kofile, and it points visitors to the Ohio Recorders' Association site for more fee information. The office keeps the record of land ownership and of every lien against it, which is why a clean recorded deed matters to the next buyer.

sections.h2: Hardin County housing at a glance
sections.html:
Hardin County is small and mostly rural. The population has slipped from 32,058 in 2010 to 30,696 at the 2020 count and about 30,072 by July 2025. Owners occupy 74.7% of homes (2020 to 2024), and the typical owner-reported home value is $151,200. Median gross rent is $793, and the county has 12,944 housing units.

With a falling population and many single-person households, a house can sit listed for a while. A sale to someone paying cash and closing at a local title office still ends with the same Auditor stamp and the same Recorder filing, so the deed steps below apply to either route.

sections.h2: Why the Auditor's stamp comes first
sections.html:
A mailed conveyance is taken only when the Auditor's stamp is already on it. The office will not walk a conveyance through the map department and the Auditor's office for you.

That sets the order: map department and Auditor first, Recorder last. A seller who mails a deed straight to the Recorder should expect it to come back unrecorded. A seller who lives far away can hand that errand to the attorney or title agent running the closing.

On the Auditor's forms page you will find the DTE 100 value statement, the DTE 100EX exemption statement and the DTE 101 homestead conveyance statement, with a reminder to confirm the newest version with the Ohio Department of Taxation.

sections.h2: What recording costs in Hardin County
sections.html:
The recording fee comes from state statute. ORC 317.32 builds the opening pair of pages from a $17 base fee and a $17 housing trust fund fee, with $4 and $4 for each page that follows. A county may also charge a document preservation surcharge of up to $5.

State fee schedule for recording
ServiceFee
Recording, opening two pages$34.00 (surcharge up to $5.00 may apply)
Recording, each additional page$8.00
Marginal notation$4.00
Certified copy$2.00 per page and $1.00 per seal
Document not meeting format standard$20.00
Release of federal lien$3.00

Call the Recorder at either number to learn exactly what the county adds per document, and keep the receipt with your closing papers. Pay the Recorder for recording, and expect separate Auditor charges.

The seller signs and then acknowledges the deed in front of an authorized official. Under ORC 5301.01 that can be a judge or clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor, who certifies the acknowledgment.

Many sellers visit a notary at a title company or bank. The deed then goes to the Auditor with a completed DTE 100, or a DTE 100EX for an exempt transfer. Ask the Hardin County Auditor for the conveyance rate and per-parcel transfer fee before closing.

ORC 317.114 sets the page format here as in every Ohio county: legible print, black or blue ink, no highlighting, and empty space at the head of the page for county stamps.

Manufactured or mobile homes that are taxed like real property use their own set of forms. The Auditor posts a registration certificate (DTE 41), a conveyance fee statement of value and receipt (DTE 100M), and an exemption statement (DTE 100MEX) for that category.

A refund or waiver application for destroyed or damaged manufactured homes (DTE 49) is posted too. When the home sits on land you own, ask the Auditor whether your sale takes the real property forms, the manufactured home forms, or both.

The Real Estate section adds the 2 1/2% reduction application (DTE 105C), the valuation complaint (DTE 1) and a deduction application for damaged or destroyed property (DTE 26). Ask about the 2 1/2% reduction at closing if the buyer will make the house a primary home.

sections.h2: Tax dates that affect a sale
sections.html:
The Auditor describes a full reappraisal of real property every six years with an update every three. Find out where your parcel sits in that cycle, because a new value can change the tax bills a buyer inherits.

On the Auditor's calendar, February 11 is the last day to pay the first half of the real estate bill without penalty and July 8 is the last day for the second half. The Board of Revision complaint period opens January 3 and closes March 31. Homestead and 2 1/2% rollback applications are due in early June. Check your tax bill for exact dates, since weekends and holidays can move them.

  • Learn from the closing agent how taxes will be prorated.
  • Ask whether the parcel has a homestead reduction, because DTE 101 then travels with the deed.
  • Photograph the stamped deed before it goes to the Recorder.

sections.h2: What to bring to the courthouse
sections.html: Bring the signed and acknowledged deed, the completed DTE form, and a check for the Auditor's fees. If the land has a homestead reduction, add the DTE 101. If it has an agricultural valuation, ask whether another statement is needed. Know the parcel number and the legal description from your own deed, since the map department compares the new description against the old one. A new description that differs from the prior deed can get a deed sent back.

sections.h2: Order of steps for a Hardin County sale
sections.html:
Have the deed prepared by an attorney or title agent and signed before a notary. Visit the map department and the Auditor in Suite 250 with the DTE form and the fees. Walk the stamped deed to Suite 220 and pay the recording fee. If you mail it, make sure the Auditor's stamp is already on it and include a return envelope.

Once recorded, the deed is indexed in the online search, which a later title examiner will read. If you paid off a mortgage on the property, check that the release was recorded too. A missing release is a common reason a closing stalls, and the lender is the one who has to fix it.

faqs.q: Can a deed go by mail to the Hardin County Recorder?
faqs.a: Only if the Auditor's stamp is already on it. Without that stamp the Recorder's Office will not take the conveyance, and staff will not walk deeds through the map department or Auditor.

faqs.q: When is the Hardin County Recorder open?
faqs.a: It opens at half past eight each weekday morning and closes at 4:00 p.m., at One Courthouse Square, Suite 220 in Kenton.

faqs.q: Who can notarize a deed in Ohio?
faqs.a: Under ORC 5301.01 a notary public, a county auditor, a county engineer, a mayor, or a judge or clerk of a court of record can take the acknowledgment. Most sellers use a notary.

faqs.q: Is there a Hardin County online records search?
faqs.a: Yes. The Recorder's page links to an online service and search provided through Kofile.

faqs.q: Who tells me the Hardin County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The Auditor, at 419-674-2239. That office collects the conveyance and transfer fees before the deed moves on to the Recorder.
